summary:
In space, the most consequential health changes are often those an astronaut cannot feel, but intervention from Earth may not arrive in time. Designed as an on-board health monitoring and clinical decision-support platform for crew self-reliance, ASTRA puts health intelligence directly in the astronaut's hands.

Before the mission, ASTRA establishes an astronaut's preflight baseline, with every measurement in orbit and during recovery compared against the astronaut's own normal physiology rather than standard Earth averages. Alongside core vital signs (heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, and body temperature), dedicated modules track five risks that often go unnoticed: silent neck-vein clots, fainting risk upon landing, carbon dioxide buildup during sleep, medicines losing strength, and cumulative radiation exposure. A private, personalized companion also supports mental wellbeing through brief daily check-ins, objective reaction tests, and tailored guidance to counter prolonged isolation.

ASTRA evaluates crew health, compares individual readings across the entire crew to distinguish a personal medical issue from a shared cabin problem, and provides a clear action plan or structured report for the flight surgeon. Built on NASA, NOAA, and open-sources physiological datasets, ASTRA creates autonomous medical support for future exploration missions.
details:
What exactly does it do?

ASTRA (Autonomous System for Telemetry, Risk, and Assessment) is a continuous, personalized health monitoring and clinical decision-support platform designed for crew self-reliance during spaceflight. Rather than relying on scheduled check-ups or on an astronaut noticing subtle symptoms, ASTRA tracks body measurements, cabin conditions and psychological wellbeing, and flags changes from an individual’s own preflight normal before they become emergencies.

Alongside core vital signs like heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose and body temperature, ASTRA monitors five spaceflight risks that are silent or slow to appear:

  • Silent neck-vein clots: Monitors internal jugular vein blood flow via guided ultrasound to catch asymptomatic clots early.
  • Fainting risk upon landing: Tracks cardiovascular deconditioning to predict and prevent post-flight dizziness or fainting when re-entering gravity.
  • Carbon dioxide buildup during sleep: Flags localized cabin airflow issues and nocturnal CO2 spikes that impair rest and morning alertness.
  • Medicines losing strength: Tracks onboard drug shelf-life and environmental exposure to warn of reduced potency.
  • Cumulative radiation exposure: Monitors ongoing space radiation doses against mission and career safety limits.

To support mental health, ASTRA pairs a private companionship mini-bot with a daily mood check-in and an objective reaction-time test, keeping all personal responses strictly confidential to each astronaut. Using these results, the companion offers tailored, conversational guidance to help crew members manage prolonged isolation and disrupted sleep.

How It Works

  1. Preflight baseline: In the 30 days before launch, ASTRA records each astronaut’s resting heart rate, sleep patterns, mood, reaction speed, stand-test results and six baseline ultrasound scans of the eyes, jugular vein and heart.
  2. In-flight monitoring: On every mission day, wearable and cabin sensor readings are compared with the astronaut’s personal baseline rather than population averages, and ASTRA prompts guided ultrasound self-scans and a brief check-in on a schedule modelled on NASA protocols.
  3. Cross-crew comparison: When a reading is unusual, ASTRA compares it across all four crew members to distinguish an individual medical issue from a shared cabin or life-support fault.
  4. Tiered alerts: Green readings sit within the personal baseline and NASA-STD-3001 limits. Amber readings show a clear shift from the astronaut’s own baseline; they appear on a body map with a plain-language explanation and remain private unless the astronaut chooses to share them. Red readings exceed safety limits and are sent automatically to flight surgeons with a structured report and the ultrasound images.

Key Benefits:

  • Detects symptom-free risks early by replacing reliance on reported symptoms with routine screening for change.
  • Reduces false alarms by comparing each astronaut with their own preflight baseline instead of population averages.
  • Supports crews through deep-space communication delays by providing immediate decision support and clear action plans.
  • Separates human illness from equipment faults by comparing unusual readings across the whole crew.
  • Protects psychological safety by keeping mood data and amber changes private to the astronaut.

Intended Impact

In the short term, ASTRA aims to move from simulated crew profiles to real data by connecting a wearable device and testing its baseline and alert model on live readings. In the long term, ASTRA is intended to become an onboard system that runs alongside mission-control software, giving crews on missions to the Moon and Mars the means to detect and act on health changes without waiting for Earth.


Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, or Software used

Development Tools: Git, GitHub CLI, Node.js 24, Python 3.12 (pip), PowerShell, Git Bash, Claude Code, Playwright, headless Chromium

Infrastructure & Hosting: Vercel, GitHub, unpkg CDN, Google Fonts

Browser APIs: Fetch, Web Bluetooth, localStorage, sessionStorage, ResizeObserver, Pointer Events

Live Data APIs: NASA ISS Live (Lightstreamer), NASA DONKI, NOAA SWPC GOES proton-flux, Where the ISS at? REST API, Gemini 2.5 Flash API

Frontend & UI: Vanilla JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3, inline SVG, custom SVG chart & 2D anatomical body modules, Inter typeface, Lightstreamer Web Client 9.2.3

Programming Languages: JavaScript, Python, HTML, CSS, GLSL, PowerShell, Bash

SI & Machine Learning: Gemini 2.5 Flash API (crew companionship mini-bot), ElevenLabs.io (text-to-speech)

Data Processing: Python data bundling scripts, NumPy, Pillow, per-person baseline medians, rule-based anomaly thresholds, rolling telemetry buffers

Software & Media Production: Three.js r160, FFmpeg 9, Piper 1.8, Playwright frame rendering, Python procedural audio synthesis

Hardware & Sensors (Data Inputs): CSA Bio-Monitor shirt, ISS Ultrasound 2, Butterfly iQ ultrasound, Heart Rate Monitor 2, CEVIS cycle ergometer, Actiwatch Spectrum, Major Constituent Analyzer, Timepix, TEPC, DosTel radiation instruments, Crew Active Dosimeters, Bluetooth heart-rate strap.

How It Is Creative

ASTRA treats crew health as one connected system rather than sets of separate measurements. Instead of judging readings against a general standard, it measures each astronaut against their own normal range and checks unusual results against the rest of the crew before flagging a medical problem. It also links separate parts of the mission together: recorded radiation exposure adjusts how far each stored medicine can be trusted, and sleep and reaction-test results are read against the previous night's cabin air. 

By combining personal baselines, crew-wide context, and cross-system links, ASTRA catches five subtle risks that are easy to miss—silent neck-vein clots, fainting on landing, carbon dioxide buildup during sleep, medicines losing strength, and cumulative radiation exposure, acting early before minor shifts become mission emergencies.

Factors Considered

  • Keeps mood data private so that crews can report honestly without fear of losing flight duty.
  • Pairs every self-report with an objective check, since people often feel fine when measurements show otherwise.
  • Sources every threshold, labels simulated data, and returns “repeat” for a poor-quality scan.
  • Supports decisions without diagnosing, with thresholds not yet validated in astronauts.
  • Avoids reading emotion from faces or voices, scoring mental health as one number, or turning mood tracking into a game.
projectRefs: Surveillance for jugular venous thrombosis in astronauts (Pavela et al., 2022)
